subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on variables, errors and uncertainty in a required practical, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain the difference between accuracy, precision and resolution for GCSE Physics simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is the independent variable in an experiment?
options: A variable that changes randomly
The variable you deliberately change
A variable kept constant to make the test fair
The variable you measure as the outcome
questions.explain: The independent variable is the one you deliberately change. The dependent variable is what you measure in response, and control variables are kept the same to keep the test fair.

questions.q: In an experiment stretching a spring by hanging masses on it and measuring extension, what is the dependent variable?
options: The temperature of the room
The extension of the spring
The type of spring used
The mass added to the spring
questions.explain: The extension is measured in response to the added mass, so it is the dependent variable. The mass (or force) is the independent variable that is changed.

questions.q: Why are control variables kept the same throughout an experiment?
options: To create random errors
To make sure the test is fair, so only the independent variable affects the result
To make the experiment quicker
To increase the readings
questions.explain: Control variables are kept constant so that any change in the dependent variable can be attributed only to the independent variable. This makes it a fair, valid test.

questions.q: Which instrument is most suitable for measuring the small extension of a spring accurately?
options: A millimetre ruler (measuring to the nearest mm)
A stopwatch
A measuring cylinder
A metre rule read to the nearest cm
questions.explain: A ruler with a millimetre scale gives a smaller resolution (nearest mm) than a metre rule read to the nearest cm, so it measures small extensions more precisely.

questions.q: A measurement is described as accurate when it is:
options: given to many decimal places
taken quickly
repeated many times
close to the true (accepted) value
questions.explain: An accurate measurement is one that is close to the true or accepted value. Accuracy is about correctness, not about how many times a reading is repeated.

questions.q: A set of repeated measurements is described as precise when the values are:
options: taken with expensive equipment
always whole numbers
all very close to one another (little spread)
close to the true value
questions.explain: Precise measurements are grouped closely together with little spread, regardless of whether they are close to the true value. Precision is about consistency, not correctness.

questions.q: A true value is 20.0 cm. Set X gives 19.9, 20.0, 20.1 cm. Set Y gives 22.1, 22.0, 22.2 cm. Which best describes the sets?
options: X is both precise and accurate; Y is precise but not accurate
X is precise but not accurate; Y is accurate but not precise
X is neither; Y is both
X is accurate but not precise; Y is precise and accurate
questions.explain: Set X values are close together (precise) and near 20.0 cm (accurate). Set Y values are close together (precise) but far from 20.0 cm (not accurate).

questions.q: The resolution of a measuring instrument is:
options: how close a reading is to the true value
the number of times a reading is repeated
the smallest change in the quantity that it can detect or show
the largest value it can measure
questions.explain: Resolution is the smallest change in the measured quantity that produces a change in the reading. For example, a ruler marked in mm has a resolution of 1 mm.

questions.q: A digital balance reads to 0.01 g. What is its resolution?
options: 1 g
questions.explain: The smallest change the balance can show is 0.01 g, so its resolution is 0.01 g.

questions.q: Results are described as repeatable when:
options: only one measurement is taken
the same person, using the same method and equipment, gets similar results when repeating the measurement
the results match the textbook value
a different person gets similar results with different equipment
questions.explain: Repeatable means the same experimenter, using the same method and equipment, obtains similar results when repeating the measurement. Reproducible means others get similar results using different equipment or methods.

questions.q: Results are described as reproducible when:
options: different people or different equipment/methods give similar results
the same person repeats them and gets the same answer
the experiment is only done once
the readings are taken to many decimal places
questions.explain: Reproducible results are obtained when the investigation is repeated by another person, or with different equipment or techniques, and similar results are found. This gives strong evidence the results are valid.

questions.q: Which statement describes a random error?
options: It always makes readings too large
It can be removed completely by using a better scale
It shifts every reading by the same fixed amount
It causes readings to scatter unpredictably above and below the true value
questions.explain: Random errors cause unpredictable scatter in readings, both above and below the true value. Their effect can be reduced by taking repeats and calculating a mean.

questions.q: How can the effect of random error on a result be reduced?
options: By repeating readings and calculating a mean
By reading the scale from an angle
By taking a single careful reading
By using a smaller sample only once
questions.explain: Because random errors scatter above and below the true value, repeating measurements and taking a mean reduces their overall effect on the final result.

questions.q: A systematic error:
options: scatters readings randomly around the true value
affects all readings by the same amount or in the same direction
only happens once during an experiment
is reduced by taking a mean of repeats
questions.explain: A systematic error affects readings consistently, shifting them all in the same direction (or by the same amount). Taking a mean does NOT remove it; the cause must be corrected.

questions.q: A force meter (newtonmeter) reads 0.2 N when nothing is hanging on it. This is an example of:
options: an anomalous result
good precision
a random error
a zero error (a type of systematic error)
questions.explain: An instrument that does not read zero when it should has a zero error. It is a systematic error because it shifts every reading by 0.2 N. It should be corrected by subtracting 0.2 N or re-zeroing.

questions.q: In the results 4.1, 4.2, 4.0, 7.8, 4.1 (all in cm), which value is the anomaly and what should you do?
options: 7.8; identify it as anomalous and ignore it when calculating the mean
4.0; include it in the mean
There is no anomaly; use all values
4.2; repeat the whole experiment
questions.explain: 7.8 cm does not fit the pattern of the other values, so it is an anomalous result. Anomalies should be identified and excluded (ignored) when calculating the mean, ideally after checking for a cause.

questions.q: Repeated readings give a range from 4.0 cm to 4.2 cm. What is a reasonable estimate of the uncertainty (as +/- half the range)?
questions.explain: The range is 4.2 - 4.0 = 0.2 cm. A common estimate of uncertainty is half the range: 0.2 / 2 = 0.1 cm, so the result is quoted as +/- 0.1 cm.

questions.q: When plotting results on a graph, a line of best fit should:
options: always pass through the origin
join the first and last point with a ruler
pass exactly through every single point
follow the overall trend with points evenly scattered either side, ignoring anomalies
questions.explain: A line of best fit follows the general trend of the data, with roughly equal numbers of points above and below it. Anomalous points are ignored, and it does not have to touch every point or pass through the origin.

questions.q: Before carrying out a required practical, a risk assessment is used to:
options: increase the number of readings taken
identify hazards and describe how to reduce the risk of harm
improve the resolution of the equipment
make the experiment faster
questions.explain: A risk assessment identifies possible hazards (such as hot equipment or falling masses) and states control measures to reduce the risk of harm to the experimenter and others.

questions.q: In the OCR practical determining the density of a solid, which measurements are combined?
options: Mass (from a balance) and volume (from measurements or displacement), using density = mass / volume
Temperature and time
Only the mass
Only the length
questions.explain: Density = mass / volume. You measure the mass with a balance and the volume either from its dimensions (regular shape) or by displacement of water (irregular shape), then divide.

specSource: OCR GCSE (9–1) Physics (Gateway A) (J249) specification; Practical Skills
